* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

## Nobel Prize Winners in Science

* **Marie Sklodowska Curie (Physics, 1903 and Chemistry, 1911)** [Marie Curie](/encyclopedia/people/science/physics/joliotcurie) is considered the most famous of all women scientists. She was the only woman ever to win two Nobel Prizes. By the time she was 16, Marie had already won a gold medal at the Russian lycée in Poland upon the completion of her secondary education. In 1891, almost penniless, she began her education at the Sorbonne in Paris. In 1903 her discovery of radioactivity earned her the Nobel Prize in physics. In 1911 she won it for chemistry.

|  |
| --- |
| Marie Curie AIP Niels Bohr Library |

* **Irene Curie (Chemistry, 1935)** [Irene Curie](/encyclopedia/arts/bios/french-lit/nemirovsky-irene) was the daughter of Marie Curie. She furthered her mother's work in radioactivity and won the Nobel Prize for discovering that radioactivity could be artificially produced.
* **Gerty Radnitz Cori (Physiology or Medicine, 1947)** Gerty Cori was the first American woman to win a Nobel Prize in science. She studied enzymes and hormones, and her work brought researchers closer to understanding diabetes. She won the Nobel Prize for discovering the enzymes that convert glycogen into sugar and back again to glycogen.
* **Maria Goeppert Mayer (Physics, 1963)** Maria researched the structure of atomic nuclei. During World War II she worked on isotope separation for the atomic bomb project.
* **Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin (Chemistry, 1964)** Dorothy discovered the structures of penicillin and vitamin B(12). She won the Nobel Prize for determining the structure of biochemical compounds essential to combating pernicious anemia.
* **Rosalyn Sussman Yalow (Physiology or Medicine, 1977)** Rosayln Yalow won the Nobel Prize for developing radioimmunoassay, a test of body tissues that uses radioactive isotopes to measure the concentrations of hormones, viruses, vitamins, enzymes, and drugs.
* **[Barbara McClintock](/encyclopedia/science/bios/genetics/mcclintock-barbara) (Physiology or Medicine, 1983)** Barbara McClintock studied the chromosomes in corn/maize and her work uncovered antibiotic-resistant bacteria and a possible cure for African sleeping sickness.
* **Rita Levi-Montalicini (Physiology or Medicine, 1986)** Rita is an Italian neuroembryologist known for her co-discovery in 1954 of nerve growth factor, a previously unknown protein that stimulates the growth of nerve cells and plays a role in degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease. She received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1986.
* **Gertrude Elion (Physiology or Medicine, 1988)** Gertrude Elion is the only woman inventor inducted into The Inventors Hall of Fame. She invented the leukemia-fighting drug 6-mercaptopurine. Her continued research led to Imuran, a derivative of 6-mercaptopurine that blocks the body's rejection of foreign tissues.
* **Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard (Physiology or Medicine, 1995)** Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard won the Nobel Prize using the fruit fly to help explain birth defects in humans.
* **Linda Buck (Physiology or Medicine, 2004)** Buck and fellow American Richard Axel discovered how the olfactory system—the sense of smell—works and how people are able to recognize and remember more than 10,000 odors.
* **Françoise Barré-Sinoussi (Physiology or Medicine, 2008)** Barré-Sinoussi won the Nobel Prize with [Luc Montagnier](/biographies/science-technology/luc-montagnier) (both France) for their discovery of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
* **Elizabeth H. Blackburn and Carol W. Greider (Physiology or Medicine, 2009)** Blackburn and Greider, both of the U.S., along with fellow American Jack W. Szostak, won the Nobel Prize for their "discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase"

method.instructions: Translate X and Y into precise eligibility tests, including exclusions and time boundaries. Maintain two deduplicated candidate frontiers, one surfaced from X and one from Y, plus a ledger of verified, rejected, and unresolved identities. Begin with one search focused on each predicate and one conjunction search, sequentially so results inform the next query. Cross-match the frontiers, but verify identity and both conditions rather than treating name overlap as proof. Alternate short discovery and check_candidates rounds. Partition discovery by source, subtype, geography, era, or alphabet only where meaningful; include less obvious eligible subtypes rather than repeatedly rephrasing a successful query. Measure newly verified items per spend and new plausible candidates per search. Favor the more productive frontier while keeping a small reverse-side gap check. After two searches add no plausible candidates, change partition, provider, or frontier instead of repeating. Keep at least 35% of the initial budget for checking and evidence resolution; stop discovery earlier if the pending queue needs it. Submit only evidenced intersections, deduplicated at the hunt's entity level; do not claim completeness from search saturation alone.
method.routing_rules: Run baseline discovery on Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results. Use Exa alone for batched check_candidates, explicitly requesting both eligibility tests and identity-matched evidence. Once baseline frontiers are sampled, allow one Exa discovery probe on the weaker frontier if affordable; retain it for further discovery only if it adds useful candidates or unique evidence. Compare marginal outcomes, recognizing provider attribution is overlapping and the initial yield sample is small. Use Parallel for cheap exact-name follow-ups and Exa for consequential unresolved checks; do not repeat settled checks. Budget every variant separately and never trigger broad auto-routing. Exact checks may use 4 results; discovery remains at 8. Apply authoritative-domain filters to evidence checks, not the entire discovery frontier. Use date filters only when logically appropriate, not as a substitute for checking event or effective dates.
method.fetch_policy: Fetch only when summaries leave material eligibility or identity uncertain, or when a discovered list offers several new candidates.
